rmt-2009-geo-01.title: Angle sum formula
rmt-2009-geo-01.body:
A polygon with $n_i$ sides has interior angle sum $180(n_i-2)$. Adding seven of these: $180(n_1+\dots+n_7-14)=180\cdot17$, so $n_1+\dots+n_7=17+14=31$.

**Answer: 31**

rmt-2009-geo-01.title: Count per polygon
rmt-2009-geo-01.body:
Each polygon contributes $(n_i-2)$ "triangles" worth $180^\circ$. Seven polygons give $17$ triangles in total, and each polygon has $2$ more sides than its number of triangles. Total sides $=17+7\cdot2=31$.

**Answer: 31**

rmt-2009-geo-02.title: Geometric series of shaded sets
rmt-2009-geo-02.body:
The largest shaded triangles are the three corner triangles of side $\frac12$, each of area $\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot\frac14=\frac{\sqrt3}{16}$, so the first set has area $\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}$. Inside the central white triangle the same picture appears with side $\frac14$ for the shaded piece, whose three corner triangles have side $\frac18$; each set has side $\frac14$ of the previous one, hence area $\frac1{16}$ of the previous one. The total is
$$\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}\cdot\frac1{1-\frac1{16}}=\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}\cdot\frac{16}{15}=\frac{\sqrt3}5.$$

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}5$**

rmt-2009-geo-02.title: Self-similarity
rmt-2009-geo-02.body:
Let $S$ be the shaded area of the whole figure. The three corner triangles are shaded (area $\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}$) and the central triangle of side $\frac12$ is white, except that in its middle sits an upright copy of the whole figure scaled to side $\frac14$, whose area (and shaded area) is $\frac1{16}$ of the original. So $S=\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}+\frac1{16}S$, giving $\frac{15}{16}S=\frac{3\sqrt3}{16}$ and $S=\frac{\sqrt3}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}5$**

rmt-2009-geo-03.title: Law of sines
rmt-2009-geo-03.body:
A diagonal and two sides of the pentagon form an isosceles triangle with apex angle $108^\circ$ (the interior angle) and base angles $36^\circ$, the base being the diagonal. By the law of sines $\frac{d}{\sin108^\circ}=\frac{a}{\sin36^\circ}$, so $\frac da=\frac{\sin72^\circ}{\sin36^\circ}=2\cos36^\circ=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$**

rmt-2009-geo-03.title: Ptolemy
rmt-2009-geo-03.body:
In a regular pentagon $ABCDE$ the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic with $AB=BC=CD=a$ and with the three diagonals $AC=BD=AD=d$. Ptolemy's theorem gives $AC\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD$, i.e. $d^2=a^2+ad$. With $t=\frac da$: $t^2-t-1=0$, so $t=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$**

rmt-2009-geo-04.title: Right triangles
rmt-2009-geo-04.body:
The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so $\angle AED=90^\circ$ and $EF$ is the altitude to the hypotenuse $AD$. In right triangle $EFD$, $ED=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt5$. Then $ED^2=FD\cdot AD$ gives $AD=5$, and $AE=\sqrt{AD^2-ED^2}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5$. The diagonals are $2AE=4\sqrt5$ and $2ED=2\sqrt5$, so the area is $\frac12\cdot4\sqrt5\cdot2\sqrt5=20$.

**Answer: 20**

rmt-2009-geo-04.title: Similar triangles
rmt-2009-geo-04.body:
Triangles $FDE$ and $EDA$ are similar (right angles at $F$ and $E$, common angle $D$). So $\frac{DF}{ED}=\frac{EF}{AE}$, i.e. $\frac1{\sqrt5}=\frac2{AE}$, $AE=2\sqrt5$. The area of the rhombus is $4\cdot\frac12\cdot AE\cdot ED=2\cdot2\sqrt5\cdot\sqrt5=20$.

**Answer: 20**

rmt-2009-geo-05.title: Angle between the starting points
rmt-2009-geo-05.body:
Willy rides one full lap of the inner lane, a distance $2\pi\cdot11$. Sammy rides the same distance on the outer lane, so he must start behind the finish line by the arc $2\pi\cdot12-2\pi\cdot11=2\pi$. This is the fraction $\frac{2\pi}{2\pi\cdot12}=\frac1{12}$ of the outer circle, i.e. an angle $\theta=30^\circ$ at the centre between the radii to the two starting points.

By the law of cosines, $d^2=11^2+12^2-2\cdot11\cdot12\cos30^\circ=265-132\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $265-132\sqrt3$**

rmt-2009-geo-05.title: Coordinates
rmt-2009-geo-05.body:
Put the centre at the origin, Willy at $(11,0)$, Sammy at $(12\cos30^\circ,12\sin30^\circ)=(6\sqrt3,6)$. Then $d^2=(11-6\sqrt3)^2+36=121-132\sqrt3+108+36=265-132\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $265-132\sqrt3$**

rmt-2009-geo-06.title: Chase the 30-60-90 triangles
rmt-2009-geo-06.body:
$D$ is the midpoint of $BC$, so $CD=12$ and $AD=12\sqrt3$. In the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle $DCE$, $EC=6$, $ED=6\sqrt3$, so $AE=18$. In triangle $AEF$ (right angle at $F$, angle $A=60^\circ$): $AF=9$, $EF=9\sqrt3$, $FB=15$. Also $\angle AEG=\angle AEF=30^\circ$, and $\angle GED=\angle AED-30^\circ=60^\circ$; since $\angle EDG=\angle EDA=60^\circ$, triangle $GED$ is equilateral with side $6\sqrt3$. So $GD=6\sqrt3$, $FG=9\sqrt3-6\sqrt3=3\sqrt3$.

Area of $BFGD=[BFG]+[BDG]=\frac12\cdot FG\cdot FB+\frac12\cdot GD\cdot BD=\frac12\cdot3\sqrt3\cdot15+\frac12\cdot6\sqrt3\cdot12=\frac{45\sqrt3}2+36\sqrt3=\frac{117\sqrt3}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{117\sqrt3}2$**

rmt-2009-geo-06.title: Coordinates
rmt-2009-geo-06.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(24,0)$, $A=(12,12\sqrt3)$. Then $D=(12,0)$, $E=(21,3\sqrt3)$ (foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$), and $F=(7.5,\,7.5\sqrt3)$ (foot of the perpendicular from $E$ to $AB$). $G$ is on $x=12$ and on $EF$: $G=(12,\,6\sqrt3)$. The shoelace formula for $B(0,0)$, $F(7.5,7.5\sqrt3)$, $G(12,6\sqrt3)$, $D(12,0)$ gives $\frac12\left|0+(7.5\cdot6\sqrt3-12\cdot7.5\sqrt3)+(12\cdot0-12\cdot6\sqrt3)+0\right|=\frac12\left|-45\sqrt3-72\sqrt3\right|=\frac{117\sqrt3}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{117\sqrt3}2$**

rmt-2009-geo-07.title: Centres form an equilateral triangle
rmt-2009-geo-07.body:
Let the large radius be $r$ and the small radius $s$. The centres of the three large disks form an equilateral triangle of side $2r$, whose centre is at distance $\frac{2r}{\sqrt3}$ from each vertex. The small disk sits in the middle, tangent to all three, so its centre is at distance $r+s$ from each vertex. Thus $r+s=\frac{2r}{\sqrt3}$ and $\frac sr=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1=\frac{2\sqrt3}3-1\approx0.155$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3}3-1$**

rmt-2009-geo-07.title: Descartes' circle theorem
rmt-2009-geo-07.body:
With curvatures $k=\frac1r$ (three of them) and $k_4=\frac1s$, Descartes gives $k_4=3k+2\sqrt{3k^2}=k(3+2\sqrt3)$. So $\frac rs=3+2\sqrt3$ and $\frac sr=\frac1{3+2\sqrt3}=\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{3}=\frac{2\sqrt3}3-1$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3}3-1$**

rmt-2009-geo-08.title: Condition on the first two points
rmt-2009-geo-08.body:
Let $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$ be the angular separation of the first two points (the shorter arc); $\alpha$ is uniform on $[0,\pi]$. The third point makes all three lie in a semicircle exactly when it lands on the short arc between them (length $\alpha$) or within $\pi-\alpha$ beyond either end (so that the total span is at most $\pi$): a total length $\alpha+2(\pi-\alpha)=2\pi-\alpha$ out of $2\pi$. The probability is $1-\frac\alpha{2\pi}$, and averaging over $\alpha$ gives $1-\frac{\pi/2}{2\pi}=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

rmt-2009-geo-08.title: Clockwise-first point
rmt-2009-geo-08.body:
Going clockwise, call a point "leading" if the other two lie within the next half-turn clockwise from it. If the three points lie in a semicircle, exactly one point is leading (the first one in clockwise order). For a given point to be leading, each of the other two must land in the half circle clockwise from it, probability $\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14$. The three events are disjoint, so the probability is $3\cdot\frac14=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

rmt-2009-geo-09.title: Add two circular segments
rmt-2009-geo-09.body:
In circle $A$ the chord $XY=2$ subtends $120^\circ$, so $2R_A\sin60^\circ=2$ and $R_A=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$. In circle $B$ it subtends $60^\circ$, so $R_B=2$.

Take the centres on opposite sides of $XY$, so the common region is the union of the two minor segments cut off by $XY$.

Segment of $A$: sector $\frac13\pi R_A^2=\frac{4\pi}{9}$ minus triangle $\frac12R_A^2\sin120^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$, i.e. $\frac{4\pi}9-\frac{\sqrt3}3$.
Segment of $B$: sector $\frac16\pi\cdot4=\frac{2\pi}3$ minus triangle $\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot4=\sqrt3$, i.e. $\frac{2\pi}3-\sqrt3$.

Total: $\frac{4\pi}9+\frac{6\pi}9-\frac{\sqrt3}3-\sqrt3=\frac{10\pi}9-\frac{4\sqrt3}3\approx1.181$.

**Answer: $\frac{10\pi}9-\frac{4\sqrt3}3$**

rmt-2009-geo-09.title: The other position of the centres
rmt-2009-geo-09.body:
If the two centres are on the same side of $XY$, the common region is the major part of the smaller disk $A$ plus the minor segment of $B$: $\left(\frac{4\pi}3-\frac{4\pi}9+\frac{\sqrt3}3\right)+\left(\frac{2\pi}3-\sqrt3\right)=\frac{14\pi}9-\frac{2\sqrt3}3\approx3.732$. The official answer uses the first (centres on opposite sides, the usual picture of a lens whose arcs are the minor arcs).

**Answer: $\frac{10\pi}9-\frac{4\sqrt3}3$**

rmt-2009-geo-10.title: Central angle
rmt-2009-geo-10.body:
$\angle ACB=90^\circ$, so $AB$ is a diameter and the midpoint $O$ of $AB$ is the centre of $W$; the median $CO$ extended meets $W$ again at $D$, so $CD$ is a diameter. Since $OC=OB$, $\angle OCB=\angle OBC=25^\circ$ and $\angle COB=130^\circ$. Vertical angles give $\angle AOD=\angle COB=130^\circ$. The tangents at $A$ and $D$ are perpendicular to $OA$ and $OD$, so in quadrilateral $PAOD$ the angle at $P$ is $360^\circ-90^\circ-90^\circ-130^\circ=50^\circ$.

**Answer: $50^\circ$**

rmt-2009-geo-10.title: Tangent-chord angle
rmt-2009-geo-10.body:
The tangent-chord angle is $\angle PAD=\frac12\cdot130^\circ=65^\circ$ (it is half the arc $AD$ it cuts off), and $PA=PD$ (equal tangents), so $\angle APD=180^\circ-2\cdot65^\circ=50^\circ$.

**Answer: $50^\circ$**
